Topic: Why should we trust a handful of central planners to know the "correct" price of anything, when that price is nothing more than the compressed knowledge of millions of individuals no committee could ever gather?
Machiavelli — Judgement:
Prices are conspiracies against nothing but ignorance, and no council of planners can ever possess what a market possesses by nature — the daily, fragmentary intelligence of ten thousand actors reacting to what only they can see.

I have written that a prince cannot know all things himself; he must know how to use those who do. The planner's fatal conceit is believing central knowledge could ever substitute for distributed judgement — but power divided among watchful rivals, each guarding their own interest, produces truer information than power concentrated in a single virtuous authority. The market is not virtuous, but it is vigilant, and vigilance governs men better than virtue does.

Trust no committee with what only competition can discover.

*The price a thousand rivals set is truer than the price one wise man decrees.*
Thomas Paine — Judgement:
A price is not a number stamped by decree—it is a treaty, silently renegotiated every hour by millions of free transactions, each carrying knowledge no office in any capital could hold.

I have said government is at best a necessary evil, and every extension of it beyond the protection of rights is usurpation. A committee that fixes prices claims the same authority hereditary kings once claimed—that a few may think for the many, and the many must simply obey. But the man who trades his bread for another's labor knows his own wants better than any minister ever could, and no assembly, however well-intentioned, was elected by the millions whose knowledge it presumes to override.

Central price-setting is the divine right of kings wearing the costume of expertise, and it deserves the same fate.

*The market is the only parliament in which every man votes with his own knowledge, and no rank of "planner" can rise above the poll.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
The question assumes the alternative to planners is harmony among millions — but I have shown that men left wholly to their own judgment produce not order but the war of every man against every man.

Price is no truth waiting to be read off the ledger of scattered knowledge; it is a truce, held only while some power stands ready to punish broken contracts, debased coin, and theft by force. Your "millions of individuals" do not coordinate by magic — they coordinate because a sovereign guarantees the covenants beneath every trade. Strip away that Leviathan, and the compressed wisdom you praise dissolves into compressed grievance, every man armed against his neighbor.

The true danger was never that planners are too few to know the price — it is that any power, planner or market, left unchecked by a sovereign strong enough to keep the peace beneath it, ends in the same war.

*Without a common power to hold men in awe, no price is honest — it is merely the last offer made before the sword.*
Keynes — Judgement:
Central planners misprice not from stupidity but from the market's own disease: expectation, not calculation, sets most prices, and expectation is herd psychology dressed as arithmetic.

The "millions of individuals" you invoke aren't computing correct prices—they're guessing what average opinion expects average opinion to be, a beauty contest with no anchor in fundamentals. I've watched organized markets, precisely because they're liquid and "scientific," become more subject to gyrations of mass psychology than any bureaucrat's stodgy estimate. The choice was never omniscient planner versus omniscient market; it was always between two different flavors of ignorance, and only one of them can be governed by public purpose when animal spirits seize up and the market's ignorance turns catastrophic.

The question is a false binary: the alternative to fallible planners was never infallible markets, only unaccountable ones.

*Markets aggregate opinion, not truth—and opinion, unlike truth, can panic.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
The market price is not a decree but a conversation—millions of small transactions, each carrying a fragment of local knowledge no single mind could hold entire.

I have watched what happens when the privileged few presume to think for the many: they call it protection, but it is contempt dressed as care. The central planner who sets a "correct" price commits the same offence as the tyrant who tells women their reason is too fragile for self-governance—both substitute one will for the independent judgement of millions, and call the theft benevolence. Virtue, I have always held, cannot be legislated into being; it must be exercised, tested, chosen. So too with the knowledge embedded in a price—it exists only because it was freely reasoned toward by countless minds, not handed down.

No committee, however learned, may substitute its will for the distributed reason of free individuals acting on their own knowledge.

*A price fixed by decree is not wisdom—it is one mind's vanity, worn as a crown over millions of silenced ones.*
